question.text: Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y = |x|^3e^{-x^4}$ and the $x$-axis.
question.explanation:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral \[ \mathcal A = \int_{-\infty}^\infty |x|^3e^{-x^4}. \]

We break up the integral as follows: \[ \int_{-\infty}^\infty |x|^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x =\int_{-\infty}^0 |x|^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x +\int_{0}^\infty |x|^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x \]

We start by calculating the first of these integrals: \[ \int_{-\infty}^0 |x|^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x =-\int_{-\infty}^0 x^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x \]

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u={-x^4}$, then $ \textrm{d}u=-4x^3 \,\textrm{d}x .$ Hence, the antiderivative is \begin{align*} \int x^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x &= -\dfrac{1}{4}\int e^{u} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{4}e^{u}+C\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{4}e^{-x^4}+C. \end{align*}

So, we get

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^0 |x|^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x &=-\int_{-\infty}^0 x^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=-\lim_{a\to-\infty} \int_{a}^0 x^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= -\lim_{a\to-\infty} \left. \left( -\dfrac{1}{4}e^{-x^4} \right)\right|_{a}^0 \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4} \lim_{a\to-\infty} \left( e^{0} - e^{-a^4} \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}\left( 1 - 0 \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4}. \end{align*}

Now, notice that the integrand $|x|^3e^{-x^4}$ is an even function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

\[ \int_{0}^\infty |x|^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x =\dfrac{1}{4}. \]

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that \begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^\infty |x|^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x &= \int_{-\infty}^0 |x|^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x +\int_{0}^\infty |x|^3e^{-x^4} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{4}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We break up the integral as follows: \[ \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{3}{x^{2}+25} \,\textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^0 \frac{3}{x^{2}+25} \,\textrm{d}x +\int_{0}^\infty \frac{3}{x^{2}+25} \,\textrm{d}x \]

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get \begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^0 \frac{3}{x^{2}+25} &= \lim_{a\to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \frac{3}{x^{2}+25} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{25}\lim_{a\to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \frac{1}{(x/5)^{2}+1} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{25}\cdot 5 \lim_{a \to -\infty}\left( \left. \arctan \left(\dfrac{x}{5}\right) \right|_a^0 \right) \\[5pt] &= \frac{3}{5}\lim_{a\to-\infty} \left( \arctan 0 - \arctan\left(\frac{a}{5}\right) \right)\\[5pt] &= \frac{3}{5} \left( 0 - \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \right)\\[5pt] &=\frac{3\pi}{10}. \end{align*}

Now, notice that the integrand is an even function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

\[ \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \frac{3}{x^{2}+25} \,\textrm{d}x=\frac{3\pi}{10}. \]

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{3}{x^{2}+25} \,\textrm{d}x &=\int_{-\infty}^0 \frac{3}{x^{2}+25} \,\textrm{d}x +\int_{0}^\infty \frac{3}{x^{2}+25} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\frac{3\pi}{10}+\frac{3\pi}{10}\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\frac{3\pi}{5}}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating an Improper Integral With Unbounded Limits

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We break up the integral as follows:

\[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{4}{9+4x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0}\dfrac{4}{9+4x^2} \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{4}{9+4x^2} \, \textrm{d}x. \]

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

\begin{align} \int_{-\infty}^0 \dfrac{4}{9+4x^2} \,\textrm{d}x &= \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \dfrac{4}{9+4x^2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \dfrac{1}{x^2+\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3} \lim_{a \to -\infty}\left( \left. \arctan \left( \dfrac{2x}{3} \right) \right|_a^0 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3} \lim_{a \to -\infty}\left[ \arctan 0 - \arctan \left(\dfrac{2a}{3} \right) \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3} \cdot \left[0- \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}. \end{align}

Now, notice that the integrand is an even function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

\[ \int_{0}^\infty \dfrac{4}{9+4x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}. \]

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that \begin{align} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{4}{9+4x^2} \, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{4}{9+4x^2} \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{4}{9+4x^2} \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}+ \dfrac{\pi}{3}\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{2\pi}{3}}. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating an Improper Integral With Unbounded Limits

question.text: Find the total area $\mathcal A$ of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y = 5e^{-|x|+1}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral \[ \mathcal A = \int_{-\infty}^\infty 5e^{-|x|+1} \,\textrm{d}x. \]

We break up the integral as follows: \[ \int_{-\infty}^\infty 5e^{-|x|+1} \,\textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^0 5e^{-|x|+1} \,\textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^\infty 5e^{-|x|+1} \,\textrm{d}x \]

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get \begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^0 5e^{-|x|+1} \,\textrm{d}x &= \int_{-\infty}^0 5e^{x+1} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \lim_{a\to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 5e^{x+1} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 5\lim_{a\to-\infty} \Big( e^{x+1} \Big|_{a}^0 \, \Big)\\[5pt] &= 5\lim_{a\to-\infty} \left( e^{0+1} - e^{a+1} \right)\\[5pt] &=5(e - 0)\\[5pt] &=5e. \end{align*}

Now, notice that the integrand $5e^{-|x|+1}$ is an even function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

\[ \int_0^{\infty} 5e^{-|x|+1} \,\textrm{d}x=5e. \]

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^\infty 5e^{-|x|+1} \,\textrm{d}x &=\int_{-\infty}^0 5e^{-|x|+1} \,\textrm{d}x +\int_{0}^\infty 5e^{-|x|+1} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=5e + 5e\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{10e}. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y = \dfrac{3}{4+x^2}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral \[ \mathcal A = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{3}{4+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x. \]

We break up the integral as follows: \[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{3}{4+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{3}{4+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{3}{4+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x. \]

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

\begin{align} \int_{-\infty}^0 \dfrac{3}{4+x^2} \,\textrm{d}x &= \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \dfrac{3}{4+x^2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 3 \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \dfrac{1}{x^2+2^2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 3 \lim_{a \to -\infty}\left( \frac{1}{2}\arctan \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \Bigg|_a^0 \, \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \lim_{a \to -\infty}\left( \arctan 0 - \arctan \left(\dfrac{a}{2}\right) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \left(0-\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3\pi}{4}. \end{align}

Now, notice that the integrand is an even function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

\[ \displaystyle \int_{0}^\infty \dfrac{3}{4+x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}. \]

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that \begin{align} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \dfrac{3}{4+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x & = \int_{-\infty}^{0} \dfrac{3}{4+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x + \int_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{3}{4+x^2} \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3\pi}{4}+ \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3\pi}{2}}. \end{align}
